content: Dr. M. Krishnan Nair from the Regional Cancer Centre in India, Dr. Twalib A. Ngoma from the Ocean Road Cancer Institute in Tanzania, Dr. D. M. Parkin from the Clinical Trials Service Unit and Epidemiological Studies Unit in England, and Julietta Patnick from the NHS Cancer Screening Programmes in England are among the notable contributors to this work. Additionally, Paola Pisani from the International Agency for Research on Cancer in France, You-Lin Qiao from the Cancer Institute of the Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences and Peking Union Medical College in China, Eduardo Rosenblatt and Michael Rosenthal from the International Atomic Energy Agency in Austria, Anne Lise Ryel from the Norwegian Cancer Society in Norway, Inés Salas from the University of Santiago in Chile, Hélène Sancho-Garnier from the Centre Val d’Aurelle-Paul Lamarque in France, Hai-Rim Shin from the National Cancer Center in South Korea, and José Gomes Temporão from the Ministry of Health in Brazil have also contributed significantly. Other participants include Barry D. Bultz from the Tom Baker Cancer Centre and the University of Calgary in Canada, Jon F. Kerner from the National Cancer Institute in the USA, Luiz Antônio Santini Rodrigues da Silva from the National Cancer Institute in Brazil, and observers such as Benjamin Anderson from the Breast Health Center at the University of Washington School of Medicine in the USA, Maria Stella de Sabata from the International Union Against Cancer in Switzerland, Joe Harford from the National Cancer Institute in the USA, Jo Kennelly from the National Cancer Institute of Canada, Luiz Figueiredo Mathias from the National Cancer Institute in Brazil, Les Mery from the Public Health Agency of Canada, Kavita Sarwal from the Canadian Strategy for Cancer Control, Nina Solberg from the Norwegian Cancer Society, and Cynthia Vinson from the National Cancer Institute in the USA. The module on palliative care emphasizes the importance of timely access to quality palliative care to alleviate pain and unnecessary suffering for millions of cancer patients worldwide. It provides a framework for developing effective palliative care programs within the context of national cancer control strategies. This module builds upon the comprehensive planning module, which outlines the overall process of cancer control planning. While the focus is on cancer, the module acknowledges the need for a public health approach to palliative care that addresses all age groups and various conditions requiring such care. These conditions include HIV/AIDS, congestive heart failure, cerebrovascular diseases, neurodegenerative disorders, chronic respiratory diseases, and illnesses associated with aging, among others. The principles guiding the integration of palliative care into cancer control programs are similar to those required for managing other chronic diseases. In 2005, six million people died from cancer, and without intervention, 84 million more are projected to die over the next decade. Over 70% of cancer deaths occur in lowand middle-income countries, where resources for cancer prevention, diagnosis, and treatment are often limited or unavailable. However, cancer is largely preventable, with over 40% of cases being avoidable. Many common cancers are curable if detected early and treated appropriately. Even in advanced stages, patients' suffering can be significantly alleviated with effective palliative care. The Cancer Control: Knowledge into Action guide by the World Health Organization (WHO) is a series of six modules that provide comprehensive guidance on all critical aspects of planning and implementing effective cancer control programs.
